title: Managing Strategic Leadership and Strategy Process

questions.stem: Which option is the best vision statement under Chapter 2’s criteria (purposeful, forward-looking, “to…”, customer/problem-oriented)?

options.A: To make everyday essentials reliably available to urban households, even under city constraints.
options.B: By optimising rider routing and warehouse pick rates across the city.
options.C: By becoming the market leader in quick-commerce GMV.
options.D: To deliver groceries in 12 minutes using hyperlocal dark stores.

questions.explanation: Vision defines what the firm ultimately wants to accomplish and typically begins with “to”; problem- or customer-oriented visions correlate more with long-term success than narrow product/process claims.

questions.stem: Which option is the best mission statement (what PulseCart does and how, typically “by…”)?

options.A: To make everyday essentials reliably available to urban households.
options.B: By operating micro-warehouses and a delivery network that balances speed, accuracy, and safety.
options.C: To become the fastest delivery player in the city.
options.D: By maximising order volume and rider utilisation.

questions.explanation: Mission describes what the organisation does and how it proposes to accomplish the vision; Chapter 2 distinguishes vision (“to…”) from mission (“by…”).

questions.stem: Which option is most consistent with “core values as guardrails” rather than PR language?

options.C: “We never compromise rider safety, and we disclose substitutions transparently.”
options.D: “We aim to delight customers.”

questions.explanation: Core values are ethical standards and norms that stabilise strategy and serve as guardrails during execution; merely legalistic or aspirational slogans don’t do that work.

questions.stem: PulseCart’s CEO keeps aligning goals to current constraints (static fit). Chapter 2’s risk is best captured as:

options.A: Static fit is identical to strategic intent.
options.B: Static fit builds dynamic capabilities faster than stretch goals.
options.C: Static fit is fine unless the firm is profitable.
options.D: Static fit can become strategic misfit in high-velocity environments because actions lag reality.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 warns that in fast-moving environments, static fit leads to misfit because the environment changes faster than the firm’s response.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest “strategic intent” for PulseCart (stretch goal that pervades the organisation and accelerates learning)?

options.A: Build a capability to deliver reliability under constraints (accuracy + safety + transparency) at scale across cities within 24 months.
options.C: Reduce delivery time by 30 seconds this quarter.
options.D: Maintain current SLA and avoid expansion.

questions.explanation: Strategic intent is a stretch goal that creates organisational purpose and drives learning to build core competencies, not incremental KPI tuning.

questions.stem: Given PulseCart is small and in a high-velocity market, which strategy process is most defensible in Chapter 2 terms?

options.A: Scenario planning, because only large firms can do it.
options.B: Strategy as planned emergence, because feedback loops are short and adaptation must be fast.
options.C: No planning process; pure improvisation.
options.D: Top-down strategic planning, because turbulence demands central control.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 suggests planned emergence fits smaller firms and fast-moving environments; top-down planning fits more stable contexts.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures planned emergence rather than top-down planning?

options.B: Only executives generate initiatives; others execute.
options.C: A dominant plan is created, but autonomous bottom-up initiatives can emerge and be evaluated/coordinated by top management.
options.D: Multiple futures are mapped; no initiatives are chosen.

questions.explanation: Planned emergence blends top-down direction with bottom-up initiatives and evaluation/coordination by leadership.

questions.stem: PulseCart’s substitution controversy: which is the Chapter 2 logic for why values matter strategically (not morally alone)?

options.A: Values are only for external branding.
options.C: Values are irrelevant if incentives work.
options.D: Values stabilise strategy and provide execution guardrails, especially when decisions are decentralised.

questions.explanation: Values underlie vision, provide stability, and act as guardrails during the pursuit of advantage.

questions.stem: A strong empirical association between vision statements and performance is more likely when:

options.A: The vision is customer-oriented, stakeholders are invested, and structures align with the vision.
options.B: The vision is written by consultants and kept confidential.
options.C: The vision is expressed as quarterly OKRs.
options.D: The vision is product-oriented and never changes.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 lists these conditions for a stronger vision–performance relationship.

questions.stem: Which move best reflects “strategic leadership uses influence (not just authority) in implementation”?

options.A: CEO mandates a rewrite of all team OKRs overnight.
options.B: CEO uses persuasion to align Ops/Product/Finance around the intent and trade-offs, then commits resources credibly.
options.C: CEO delegates everything to Finance.
options.D: CEO waits for the regulator’s final order.

questions.explanation: Strategic leaders draw on position power and informal influence (persuasion) to implement strategy effectively.

questions.stem: PulseCart faces a potential regulation limiting peak-hour delivery. Which approach best fits “scenario planning” logic?

options.A: Lock in one forecast and plan only for it.
options.B: Build a single dominant plan and suppress alternatives.
options.C: Develop multiple plausible regulatory/market futures and pre-commit contingent responses.
options.D: Crowdsource decisions without executive synthesis.

questions.explanation: Scenario planning is designed for uncertainty by considering multiple plausible futures (distinct from a single dominant plan).

questions.stem: The “12-minute promise” is becoming brittle as constraints rise. The most Chapter-2-consistent reframing is:

options.A: Replace vision with a mission-only statement.
options.C: Double down on speed as the sole purpose.
options.D: Shift vision to a problem-defining/customer-oriented reliability promise that preserves flexibility.

questions.explanation: Problem-defining/customer-oriented visions support strategic flexibility to meet changing needs and opportunities.

questions.stem: In planned emergence, the realised strategy is best described as:

options.A: A combination of intended and emergent strategy.
options.C: Intended strategy only.
options.D: Emergent strategy only.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 explicitly states realised strategy combines intended and emergent components under planned emergence.

questions.stem: The biggest “con” risk of planned emergence in PulseCart is:

options.B: It can create unclear communication/lines and many bottom-up ideas may be dead ends without a good evaluation process.
options.C: It only works in stable environments.
options.D: It forbids strategic intent.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 flags confusion/lack of focus and weak evaluation of emergent ideas as major downsides.

questions.stem: Which intervention is most aligned with Chapter 2’s idea that employees must feel invested in vision/values?

options.B: Keep values fixed and unknown to teams.
options.C: Annual review where employees help revise values and assess success relative to vision/mission.
options.D: Replace values with KPI dashboards.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 notes firms build commitment by involving employees in reviewing/revising values and assessing progress against vision/mission.

questions.stem: In Chapter 2 terms, MediMesh is most clearly facing:

options.C: A stable-fit environment where alignment guarantees durable advantage.
options.D: A strategic inflection point where the environment shifts faster than the firm’s current approach.

questions.explanation: Strategic inflection points arise when competitive realities shift; static fit can become misfit in high-velocity contexts like tech/health innovation.

questions.stem: Which response best addresses “strategic dissonance” (misalignment between strategy and changing reality)?

options.A: Re-test assumptions, consider alternate futures, and adjust intent/commitments before misfit hardens.
options.C: Keep execution tight on the old plan to prove discipline.
options.D: Treat new signals as noise until profits drop.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2’s logic is to navigate inflection points by noticing misfit early and adapting strategy process/assumptions, not doubling down on static alignment.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest problem-defining vision for MediMesh (not product-defining)?

options.A: To build the best AI triage model in the market.
options.B: To reduce preventable clinical deterioration by enabling timely escalation and accountable review.
options.C: By achieving FDA clearance and shipping weekly updates.
options.D: By bundling with EHR vendors.

questions.explanation: Problem-defining/customer-oriented visions preserve flexibility and correlate with long-term success more than tool-centric declarations.

questions.stem: Which option best fits a mission statement?

options.C: By deploying clinician-in-the-loop triage workflows for clinics and hospitals.
options.D: To become category leader in AI triage.

questions.explanation: Mission explains what the organisation does and how it accomplishes the vision (“by…”).

questions.stem: The board worries the CTO is overconfident (“we’ll ship our way out”). Which Chapter 2 decision-process tool most directly counters unchallenged assumptions?

options.C: Pure top-down planning.
options.D: Devil’s advocacy.

questions.explanation: Devil’s advocacy explicitly scrutinises and critiques underlying assumptions and downsides through a separate team/role.

questions.stem: Which sequence best matches the devil’s advocacy method described in Chapter 2?

options.A: Team 1 proposes; Team 2 critiques assumptions; Team 1 revises; critique repeats; agreement under executive supervision.
options.C: Everyone votes anonymously.
options.D: Two teams generate two plans; executives synthesise.

questions.explanation: That is the stepwise process shown for devil’s advocacy in the chapter.

questions.stem: If the board wants two fully developed alternative strategies (e.g., compliance-first vs speed-first) and then a synthesis, the best fit is:

options.C: Top-down planning.
options.D: No process.

questions.explanation: Dialectic inquiry begins with two teams generating alternate detailed courses (thesis/antithesis), followed by executive synthesis.

questions.stem: Which “strategic intent” is most faithful to Chapter 2 (stretch + capability-building)?

options.A: Get 10 new enterprise customers this quarter.
options.C: Build the core competency to deliver clinically accountable triage under evolving regulation, at scale, within 18 months.
options.D: Reduce cloud spend by 7%.

questions.explanation: Strategic intent is a stretch goal that pervades the firm with purpose and accelerates learning to build core competencies.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures why values must be more than “legal compliance” in MediMesh’s context?

options.A: Values slow innovation and should be avoided.
options.B: Values are identical to the mission.
options.C: Legal compliance is sufficient for long-term trust.
options.D: Ethical core values create guardrails and stability; many harmful actions can be legal yet reputation-destroying.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 emphasises ethical standards beyond mere legality and their guardrail function for long-term success.

questions.stem: MediMesh is still small, but uncertainty is high (regulation + incumbent bundling). Which process choice is most defensible?

options.A: Scenario planning to map plausible regulatory/market futures, plus rapid feedback loops internally.
options.B: No planning because planning is slow.
options.C: Only planned emergence because scenarios are for large firms.
options.D: Only top-down planning because uncertainty requires control.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 explicitly keeps scenario planning in the strategic toolkit for uncertainty; environment rate-of-change informs the choice.

questions.stem: Which is the sharpest diagnosis of “static fit” risk in MediMesh’s setting?

options.A: Static fit is optimal because healthcare is slow.
options.B: Static fit limits stretch goals and can lag shifting competitive/regulatory realities.
options.C: Static fit equals strategic intent.
options.D: Static fit guarantees core competency creation.

questions.explanation: The chapter contrasts static fit with stretch-goal learning and notes the lag problem in fast-moving contexts.

questions.stem: The CEO needs adoption and safety. Which values statement best functions as a guardrail?

options.C: “Clinical accountability first: transparency, auditability, and escalation when uncertain.”
options.D: “Never lose a deal.”

questions.explanation: Guardrail values constrain behaviour under pressure and protect long-term success; they must be lived, not marketed.

questions.stem: Which is most consistent with “strategic leaders use influence to implement”?

options.B: CEO delegates the conflict to Slack threads.
options.C: CEO waits for perfect certainty.
options.D: CEO uses persuasion to align CTO/Legal/Sales on trade-offs, then makes credible commitments.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 highlights position and informal influence (persuasion) as core to implementation.

questions.stem: If MediMesh adopts planned emergence, the realised strategy will most likely be:

options.A: A combination of intended direction and emergent initiatives.
options.C: Only what the CEO intended.
options.D: Only bottom-up experiments.

questions.explanation: The chapter defines realised strategy in planned emergence as intended + emergent strategy together.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest board-level governance move consistent with Chapter 2’s employee buy-in logic?

options.B: Mechanisms where teams periodically assess progress relative to vision/mission and surface initiatives.
options.C: Replace values with compliance checklists.
options.D: Treat culture as irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 notes tactics that build belief and investment by employees in vision/values and progress assessment.

questions.stem: Which vision is most aligned with Chapter 2’s “purpose-driven, forward-looking, problem-defining” logic?

options.A: By winning tenders through aggressive claims.
options.B: To sell modular microgrids with patented inverters.
options.C: To enable reliable, verifiable clean power for communities and industry where the central grid fails.
options.D: By maximising megawatts installed.

questions.explanation: Purpose-driven visions motivate and are stronger when customer/problem-oriented, preserving flexibility under changing needs/opportunities.

questions.stem: Which is the best mission statement?

options.C: To enable reliable, verifiable clean power where the grid fails.
options.D: By designing, installing, and monitoring modular microgrids with transparent measurement and reporting.

questions.explanation: Mission describes what the organisation does and how it accomplishes the vision (“by…”).

questions.stem: The partner urges exaggerated emissions claims. Chapter 2’s most precise objection is:

options.A: Even if not illegal, weak extralegal ethical standards make firms prone to reputation-threatening behaviour.
options.C: It is a mission problem only.
options.D: It is illegal in all cases, so values are irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 stresses that harmful behaviour may be legal; ethical standards beyond legality reduce existential risk to the firm’s reputation and future.

questions.stem: Which core values statement best functions as a “guardrail” for GridLeaf?

options.B: “We report impact claims transparently and auditably; we refuse to misstate outcomes.”
options.C: “We move fast reinforcing what investors want.”
options.D: “We will be number one.”

questions.explanation: Values are ethical standards that stabilise strategy and keep execution on track; they must guide day-to-day decisions under pressure.

questions.stem: GridLeaf faces two plausible policy futures. The planning approach most directly built for this is:

options.C: Scenario planning.
options.D: Planned emergence only, with no scenarios.

questions.explanation: Scenario planning is in the strategic toolkit for uncertainty and multiple plausible futures, distinct from a single dominant plan.

questions.stem: If GridLeaf is mid-sized and must satisfy investors and remain adaptive, which hybrid is most defensible?

options.C: A single dominant five-year plan with no revision.
options.D: Scenario planning with contingent commitments plus selective planned emergence for local experiments.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 keeps all three approaches available and links choice to rate of change; combining scenarios with adaptive initiatives is consistent with that logic.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about why customer-oriented visions correlate with performance?

options.A: They allow strategic flexibility to meet changing needs and exploit opportunities.
options.C: They substitute for strategy.
options.D: They prevent the vision from ever changing.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 explicitly links problem-defining/customer-oriented vision to flexibility and long-term success correlation.

questions.stem: GridLeaf’s COO insists on tight alignment to current resources (static fit). In turbulent policy contexts, Chapter 2’s critique is:

options.B: Static fit maintains status quo and can curtail stretch-goal capability building.
options.C: Static fit is identical to strategic intent.
options.D: Static fit is preferred only in high-velocity settings.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 contrasts static fit with strategic intent’s stretch-goal learning and capability building.

questions.stem: Which strategic intent best fits Chapter 2?

options.C: Build a core competency in verifiable microgrid performance across regulatory regimes within two years.
options.D: Reduce marketing spend.

questions.explanation: Strategic intent is a stretch goal that creates purpose and drives learning to build core competencies for advantage.

questions.stem: To reduce groupthink about “everyone exaggerates,” which tool is the cleanest fit?

options.C: Hiring more salespeople.
options.D: Devil’s advocacy.

questions.explanation: Devil’s advocacy institutionalises critique of assumptions and downsides by a separate team/role.

questions.stem: If leadership wants two teams to develop: (i) “subsidy boom strategy” and (ii) “audit crackdown strategy,” then synthesise, the best fit is:

options.C: No framework.
options.D: Devil’s advocacy.

questions.explanation: Dialectic inquiry begins with thesis/antithesis and ends with executive synthesis/choice.

questions.stem: Which is most consistent with Chapter 2’s warning about values being “PR exercises”?

options.B: Values must be lived with integrity by leadership; otherwise employees read them as lip service.
options.C: Values only apply to junior staff.
options.D: Values can be outsourced to marketing.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 stresses that values statements without leadership commitment become PR and lose behavioural force.

questions.stem: Under planned emergence, a key advantage is:

options.C: Highest strategic flexibility and buy-in, with room for emergent initiatives.
options.D: No need for intended strategy.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 lists high flexibility and employee buy-in as a major pro of planned emergence.

questions.stem: Under planned emergence, a key risk GridLeaf must manage is:

options.B: Overreliance on a single dominant plan.
options.C: Too much clarity.
options.D: Confusion and weak evaluation of bottom-up ideas, missing big opportunities or chasing dead ends.

questions.explanation: Those are explicit cons in the planned emergence comparison table.

questions.stem: Which leadership behaviour best fits Chapter 2’s view of implementation?

options.A: Using influence and persuasion to align stakeholders, then making credible commitments.
options.C: Treating ethics as separate from strategy.
options.D: Only issuing directives.

questions.explanation: Strategic leaders use position and informal influence to direct activities in implementation; they also must back vision with commitments.

questions.stem: Which strategy process choice best fits a small firm in a high-velocity environment, per Chapter 2?

options.B: Planned emergence, because feedback loops are short and adaptation is fast.
options.C: Scenario planning is forbidden for small firms.
options.D: No process at all.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 explicitly points to planned emergence for small firms in fast-changing environments; top-down planning fits stable contexts more.

questions.stem: Under planned emergence, the role of top management is best described as:

options.C: Allow bottom-up initiatives to emerge for evaluation and coordination while maintaining top-down direction.
options.D: Replace vision/mission with experiments.

questions.explanation: Planned emergence blends top-down vision with bottom-up initiatives that are evaluated and coordinated by top management.

questions.stem: CredWeave’s realised strategy, in Chapter 2 terms, will most likely be:

options.C: Emergent only.
options.D: A combination of intended and emergent strategy.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 states realised strategy combines intended and emergent strategy under planned emergence.

questions.stem: Which option is most consistent with “problem-defining/customer-oriented” vision logic (not product-defining)?

options.A: To enable fair, timely access to working-capital at the point of need for small merchants.
options.B: By integrating into every checkout in the country.
options.C: By maximising approvals.
options.D: To build the most accurate underwriting model.

questions.explanation: Customer/problem-defining visions enable flexibility and correlate with long-term success more than tool-centric claims.

questions.stem: Which option is most clearly a mission statement?

options.A: To enable fair, timely access to working-capital at the point of need.
options.B: By embedding credit rails into merchant platforms with transparent terms and risk controls.
options.C: To become the category winner.
options.D: To accelerate growth.

questions.explanation: Mission describes what the firm does and how it accomplishes the vision (“by…”).

questions.stem: The board’s fear: planned emergence becomes chaos. Which Chapter 2 “con” is most relevant?

options.A: It only works in slow-moving environments.
options.C: Unclear communication/lines can confuse employees; many bottom-up ideas may be dead ends without evaluation.
options.D: It reduces flexibility.

questions.explanation: Confusion, lack of focus, and weak evaluation of emergent ideas are explicit risks in the chapter.

questions.stem: CredWeave sees rising defaults after expansion. This is most consistent with the early stage of:

options.C: Proof that values do not matter.
options.D: Strategic inflection point risk (fit starting to slip as conditions change).

questions.explanation: Chapter 2’s inflection-point discussion highlights that alignment can become misfit as conditions shift, especially in high-velocity settings.

questions.stem: Which “strategic intent” best fits Chapter 2’s definition?

options.A: Build the core competency to scale fair, auditable underwriting across categories within 18 months, even when signals shift.
options.C: Cut support costs.
options.D: Reduce default rate by 0.5% next month.

questions.explanation: Strategic intent is a stretch goal that pervades the organisation with purpose and accelerates learning to build core competencies.

questions.stem: The data scientist proposes a sensitive feature; Compliance worries about explainability and reputation. Which values statement best acts as a guardrail?

options.B: “We use signals we can justify: transparency, auditability, and respect for customers’ dignity.”
options.C: “We never slow down.”
options.D: “We do what is legal.”

questions.explanation: Ethical core values function as guardrails to keep the firm on track while pursuing vision/mission; legality alone is insufficient for long-term resilience.

questions.stem: To test the underwriting feature proposal while limiting groupthink, the best fit is:

options.C: Devil’s advocacy.
options.D: Replace the vision.

questions.explanation: Devil’s advocacy institutionalises critique of assumptions and downsides via a separate challenger role/team.

questions.stem: If the board demands two fully developed alternatives (aggressive expansion vs controlled compliance-first), then synthesis, the best fit is:

options.C: Devil’s advocacy.
options.D: Dialectic inquiry.

questions.explanation: Dialectic inquiry explicitly runs thesis/antithesis and then executive synthesis/choice.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures Chapter 2’s view of implementation leadership?

options.A: Effective leaders use authority and persuasion/influence to direct activities in implementation.
options.C: Implementation is the same as writing a vision statement.
options.D: Implementation is operational; strategy ends at formulation.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 emphasises position and informal influence (persuasion) in implementing strategy.

questions.stem: CredWeave wants employees “invested” in purpose. Which practice is most consistent with Chapter 2?

options.B: Employees periodically review/revise values and assess success relative to vision/mission.
options.C: Replace values with financial targets.
options.D: Outsource purpose to brand teams.

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 gives examples of involving employees in values review and progress assessment against vision/mission to build belief and motivation.

questions.stem: Which option best reflects the chapter’s empirical conditions strengthening the vision–performance link?

options.A: Vision is replaced by quarterly dashboards.
options.C: Vision is customer-oriented; stakeholders are invested; structures (e.g., incentives) align with the vision.
options.D: Vision is never communicated.

questions.explanation: Those three conditions are listed in Chapter 2 as making the association more likely.

questions.stem: CredWeave’s fastest path to prevent planned emergence from becoming “random experiments” is to:

options.B: Let every team run independent strategy.
options.C: Ban bottom-up initiatives.
options.D: Keep an intended direction (vision/intent) while establishing a clear evaluation/coordination mechanism for emergent initiatives.

questions.explanation: Planned emergence needs top-down direction plus systematic evaluation/coordination; otherwise the chapter’s listed cons (confusion, dead ends) dominate.
